subject: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets

messages.author: 938d2cd6a714081f
messages.subject: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Hi!

I have a question regarding the R package "blavaan": is it possible to use blavaan for the analysis of multiple imputed datasets? I have a very small dataset with missing values, and I do not think that ML estimation would be feasible in this case. 
If it is possible to use blavaan, how would you pool the results?

I was thinking something along the lines of having a list of imputed datasets, the model as a lavaan-object, the bsem-function and lapply.

Thank you very much!

Best wishes,
Chris

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Hi Chris (and congratulations on first post),

Here are a couple initial thoughts:
- Bayesian estimation will not necessarily solve problems with small data. At least, your results may be more sensitive to the specific priors that you use.

- You don't necessarily need multiple imputation here; you could instead simply send the incomplete data to the Bayesian model. But maybe you are using multiple imputation to include auxiliary variables or something like that.

And here are some blavaan notes:
- There are currently no helper functions to fit the imputed datasets in one go. But you could do something like put all the datasets in a list, then loop through the list to fit a model to each dataset sequentially.

- If you simply have the posterior mean and sd of each parameter (for each imputed dataset), you could send these to mi.inference() from the norm package.

- You could also combine the posterior samples from all the models and summarize them together. I will soon add something to blavaan so that it is easier to access the posterior samples. But, for now, they can be accessed via (assuming "fit" is your fitted blavaan model)

fit@external$runjags$mcmc

So, say you have two models, fit1 and fit2. Then you could do this:

postsamps <- c(fit1@external$runjags$mcmc, fit2@external$runjags$mcmc)
class(postsamps) <- "mcmc.list"
summary(postsamps)


This would give you an overall summary of parameters, using both fit1 and fit2.

Ed

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Ed

I question on how JAGS handle missing data if you just give it as NA. 
Does JAGS draws expected values from the posterior, kind of like imputation for each iteration for the missing values? Or does something different, maybe more similar to FIML?

When I code missing data in Stan I have to explicitly ask it to generate the posterior draws for each iteration for missing values

Thanks

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
The NAs are passed directly to JAGS, so that the missing values are sampled from the posterior. In the future, I will make it easier to access these sampled values. For now, though, you can add this argument to your call:

jagextra = list(monitor="y")

This will probably make a long note appear about how some entries of y are non-stochastic, but it will also save the samples from the missing values. Then the samples can be accessed in the mcmc object described in my reply above (which will also be easier to access in the future).

Ed

messages.author: 938d2cd6a714081f
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Dear Ed,

thanks for your suggestions! Everything works fine now, I have my imputed datasets and I am able to loop through these datasets.

Do I understand correctly that, in case of a Bayesian analysis of mutliple imputed datasets, I do not need to pool the estimates according to Rubin's (1987) rules? Is it enough to simply combine and summarize the posterior samples of all my model runs? This would make so much things so much easier!

Best wishes,
Chris

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
I believe that Rubin's rules were designed for the situation where, in each imputed dataset, you only have a point estimate and standard error for each parameter.  If you have the full posterior sample associated with each imputed dataset, then I believe that combining the samples does the same thing without the need for special "combination" equations.

Ed

messages.author: e6c3c7d5f40131c0
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Hi Ed,

Can I pick up on this and ask for a bit more detail (or some references to follow up)? I'm being asked to explain why I haven't used multiple imputation in a growth model with blavaan. I'm fairly new to Bayes so apologies if my terminology/phrasing is sloppy. My understanding is that if you use MCMC then missing values are estimated by drawing expected values from the initial posterior distributions for parameter estimates of the model. These 'expected' missing values would in turn inform the next iteration of posteriors, which in turn would update the 'expected' missing values and so on until the iterations are complete. Is that vaguely correct? I've read the chapter in Gelman's BDA3 but the explanation is quite technical and I'm not sure to what extent it connects to what blavaan/JAGS is doing. I'm trying to get a 'distilled' sense of what's going on in blavaan that is accurate enough but simple for a non-technical reader!

thanks

andy

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Blavaan & analysis of multiple imputed datasets
parts:
Andy,

I have a paper that may help here. The "data augmentation" approach from the paper corresponds to what is happening in blavaan:

http://dx.doi.org/10.3102/1076998610375833

A pdf preprint version is available here:

http://faculty.missouri.edu/~merklee/pub/Merkle2011.pdf

I think you can say that you are doing multiple imputation, with (i) the imputation model being your growth model of interest, and (ii) new imputations being drawn at every iteration of the MCMC procedure.

Ed

On Monday, 22 February 2016 04:48:16 UTC, Ed Merkle wrote:
The NAs are passed directly to JAGS, so that the missing values are sampled from the posterior. In the future, I will make it easier to access these sampled values. For now, though, you can add this argument to your call:

jagextra = list(monitor="y")

This will probably make a long note appear about how some entries of y are non-stochastic, but it will also save the samples from the missing values. Then the samples can be accessed in the mcmc object described in my reply above (which will also be easier to access in the future).

Ed
